title: The Eminent Usefulness of the Liberal Arts
author: David B Hayes
summary: David Hayes responds to Dan Murphy's 'Recovering the Quadrivium', which argued that classical schools like Logos and Trivium School teach almost the same mathematics sequence as conventional American schools and have neglected four of the seven liberal arts. Hayes agrees with Murphy's critique and extends it: the Prussian and Committee of Ten tradition values mathematics for serving the state and industry, while Dorothy Sayers treats it as a sub-department of logic, and in both cases mathematics becomes a servile rather than liberal art. He then challenges a deeper framing within the classical movement, namely the habit of defining liberal education as 'useless' in reaction to utilitarianism. Drawing on Pieper, Aristotle's account of friendship, and Richard Feynman's attacks on rote science and algebra instruction, Hayes argues that truth is eminently useful and that an education void of truth is what is actually useless. He closes with George Stanciu's account of being transformed by Euclid's proof of the infinitude of primes, proposing that liberal education should strike, pierce, and transform students and be a common life of friendship.
points: Many classical schools still run the standard Pre-Algebra to Calculus sequence essentially unaltered from Common Core or Archimedes-style standards.
Sayers and the Committee of Ten both treat mathematics as useful for something beyond itself, which on Pieper's definition makes it a servile rather than liberal art.
Hayes rejects describing liberal education as 'useless', arguing that truth pursued for its own sake is always useful to self and civilization.
Aristotle's friendship of the good, the most useful and pleasurable kind, models what 'for its own sake' actually means.
Feynman's critiques of memorized science and rule-following algebra illustrate how utilitarian schooling becomes meaningless.
quotes: Dan Murphy explains that in his view, it is incongruous for schools in the classical movement to use almost unaltered the standard American mathematics curriculum as outlined by the Common Core State Standards for Mathematical Education or the Archimedes Standards.
For Sayers and for classical schools who swallow whole the standard sequence of mathematical instruction, mathematics is seen as merely useful for “mental discipline,” or for “practicing logic.

Sayers view of mathematics is superior to the Committee of Ten since serving the Liberal topics of the Trivium is superior to serving industry and civilization. In both cases, math is not a liberal art, but a subservient art.
Do we in the Classical Movement differ from the Common Core Standards for Schools only in the quality and type of worldview in which we propose to indoctrinate our students?
It is a false opinion to think that making the useful the primary goal of education results in a useful education.

Arguing against those who propose usefulness as a final end of education, it is tempting to define liberal education as “useless.” But this slip in terminology is in no way based on classical thought.

The defining quality of liberal education is not uselessness, the opposite of utilitarianism. The defining quality of liberal education is not pain, the opposite of pleasure. The defining quality of liberal education is the true, because the truth will liberate you (set you free).

Liberal education is to free the person from the false opinions that there is no truth, that no one is connected to any other, and that life stinks and then you die. Liberal education ought to be a common life of friendship.
